title: Measure and line height — Image Wiki
text:
Measure and line height
  The two settings that decide whether body text is comfortable — how long the lines are, and how far apart. They have to be chosen together.

  
    Termmeasure (line length) and line height (leading)
    Also calledline length, leading, line spacing, characters per line
    Not the same asline height vs font size, measure vs column width, leading vs line height
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happensThe numbersWhy there is no single right numberCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Drag a browser window from half-screen to full-screen on a plain article page. Nothing changes except the width of the text, and suddenly the page is exhausting. You catch yourself putting a finger on the screen, or scrolling so the paragraph you want sits at the top.
That is the measure — the length of a line — doing its damage. Its partner is line height, the distance from one baseline to the next, traditionally called leading because print shops slid strips of lead between rows of metal type. Google Fonts gives the concrete case: for a 10pt font, two strips of lead brought the line height to 12pt.
These are the biggest levers over body text, and the two that get set by default and never looked at again.



Google Fonts Knowledge, "Understanding measure/line length". Content owned by Google, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; cropped for this page and shared under the same licence.
One variable: the width of the block. Same typeface, same size, same leading. The first is short enough for a caption but chops prose into fragments; the second is still too short for paragraph text; the third is about right; the fourth is the one that makes you lose your place.
Look at what breaks in the fourth. It is not that the words are harder to read. It is that when you finish a line, the beginning of the next one is a long way back and slightly down, and there is nothing to aim at.


Why it happens
Reading is a series of jumps. Your eye fixates for a fraction of a second, jumps forward a few characters, fixates again. At the end of a line it makes one much bigger jump — back to the left margin and down one line. That jump is ballistic: it is launched on an estimate and lands where it lands.
That account comes from reading research rather than from any of the typography sources cited below, none of which describes the eye movement itself. They document the consequence; this is the mechanism behind it.
Butterick states the consequence directly: as line length increases, your eye has to travel farther from the end of one line to the beginning of the next, "making it harder to track your progress vertically."

45 charactersshort jump — it lands on the line you meantShort measurea single narrow column, a paperback page110 characterslong jump — line 3, 4 or 5; you re-read or skip oneLong measurea browser window dragged full-width

The leading is identical in both panels. The only change is the measure.
Follow the arrow: the jump from the end of one line to the start of the next. On the left it covers a short distance and the landing is unambiguous — the orange bar marks about one line's worth of vertical uncertainty. On the right the same jump is nearly three times as long, and the uncertainty spans three lines. You land on the wrong one, notice, and correct. Do that forty times on a page and you are tired.


That is also the reason the two settings cannot be chosen independently. A longer jump needs a bigger vertical target, and the only way to make the target bigger is more space between the lines. Google Fonts puts it in one sentence: "as our measure grows wider, so too should our line height become more open."
The numbers
For measure, Google Fonts quotes Bringhurst: "anything from 45 to 75 characters is widely regarded as a satisfactory length of line for a single-column page set in a serifed text face." Material Design suggests 40–60 for body text on screen. Butterick, working independently, says 45–90.
They disagree, and honestly rather than sloppily — Butterick writes about print documents, Bringhurst about book pages, Material about phone screens. Take 45 as the floor everyone agrees on and 75–90 as the ceiling.
Notice the unit. Characters, not pixels or inches — because, as Butterick points out, point size changes how many characters fit in an inch, while characters per line works at any size. For a rough proxy in English, Google Fonts offers "approximately — very approximately — 10 words."
For line height, the recommendation is a multiple of the font size. Google Fonts: 115–150% is where the optimum sits — and it says for Latin script, a qualification worth taking literally (Beyond Latin). Butterick: 120–145%. The two overlap almost completely, which is as much agreement as typography offers.



Google Fonts Knowledge, "Choosing a suitable line height" — too tight, just right, too open. Content owned by Google, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; cropped for this page and shared under the same licence.
The pale blue bands are the baseline grid, so you can measure the change. Left, the descenders of one line reach the ascenders of the next and the block reads as a single grey mass. Right has the opposite failure: the lines are so far apart they stop belonging to the same paragraph, and your eye has to search downwards.


Why there is no single right number
Because the right answer depends on the measure, and the measure is a moving target on screen.
Google Fonts is explicit about the responsive case: a value such as 150% for wide viewports might instead be 130% at mobile sizes, because on a narrow screen the reader's eyes do not have far to travel. That is the same mechanism, applied backwards — short jump, small target needed, tighter leading. It is a good reason to start with the narrowest viewport and work upwards.
Two other things move the number. X-height: a face that looks big for its point size (Type anatomy) fills the line more and wants more leading. Diacritics: Google Fonts notes that languages using plentiful accents need more generous leading, and the CSS Fonts spec adds the sting in the tail — for text with diacritics, too large an x-height actually decreases legibility, because the accents get cramped.
And display type inverts the rule. For a headline, a line height below the type size usually looks better — Google Fonts suggests 90–100% for 72px type. There is no return sweep in a three-word headline, so leading only controls how the shape reads, which is Type hierarchy on a page's problem rather than this one.

45 characters65 characters100 characterstight120%normal135%open150%as the measurewidens, open upthe leadingMeasure and leading are one decision, not twothe settings that read well sit on a diagonal — there is no single correct percentage

Nine settings of the same paragraph: three measures across, three line heights down. The highlighted cells are the combinations that read well — and they sit on a diagonal, not in a column.
That diagonal is the whole article. There is no correct percentage, only a correct pairing. Move right, move down.





Google Fonts Knowledge, "Choosing a suitable line height". Content owned by Google, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; cropped for this page and shared under the same licence.
The same passage at the same font size, twice. The narrow block gets tighter leading; the wide block gets more. Count the baseline-grid marks at the right-hand edge of each line to see the difference — this is the diagonal from the previous diagram, in real type.


Common mistakes

"Line height should be a fixed number of pixels." Set it as a multiple, so it tracks the font size. Google Fonts adds an accessibility reason: if a reader scales text up and the leading is frozen, lines overlap.
"Double-spacing is generous and therefore kind." Butterick calls single and double spacing obsolete typewriter habits, and measures the presets — Word's Single, 1.5 lines and Double land near 117%, 175% and 233%, all outside the 120–145% target.
"A wide column is fine as long as the type is big." Bigger type in a wide column gives fewer characters per line, so it can help — but only until the measure is back in range. Constrain the container.
"Measure means the column width." Measure is the length of the text line. Indents, list markers and drop caps all shorten it, which is why nested lists drift out of range.
"Tight leading looks modern." It does, in a headline. In body text at a wide measure it is the fastest way to make a page feel like homework.


Checking a paragraph in fifteen seconds

Count the words in one full line. Ten is Google Fonts' very rough target; past fifteen you are almost certainly over 90 characters.
Divide the baseline-to-baseline gap by the type size. Below 1.15 or above 1.5 and you are outside the range both Google Fonts and Butterick give.
Do the descenders of one line touch anything on the line below? That is the hard floor, before taste enters.
Jump from the end of a line to the start of the next without using your finger. If you land wrong, tighten the measure or open the leading — not both.
